name: German nationalism
summary: German nationalism holds that the Germans are one nation defined by language, culture and shared history, that this nation belongs in one state with its kin across the borders, and that its language and culture must be preserved. It arose in the Napoleonic era with Fichte, Arndt and Jahn, drove the 1848 Frankfurt Assembly and the National Association, and in Wilhelmine Germany took an aggressive, racially coloured form in the Pan-German League. On the national question the strands agree; on democracy, minorities, expansion and war they split.
scope: German nationalism as a current on the national question (identity, territory, sovereignty, language, culture, minorities, kin abroad, the means it accepts): the Romantic strand (Herder, Fichte, Arndt, Jahn), the liberal-democratic strand (Hambach, the Frankfurt Assembly of 1848-49, the National Association) and the Pan-German strand (the Pan-German League, Class, the Army League). It excludes National Socialism and the Wilhelmine Empire's or Bismarck's wider policies, and treats economic and social programmes as borrowing unless the texts state them as part of the national cause.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Fichte makes a shared language the natural bond of a nation, Arndt's fatherland reaches as far as the German tongue, and the National Association and Pan-German League claim all Germans by language, blood and history across state borders.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The National Association (1860) would annex the German provinces of Austria on the ground of common blood, history and interests, and Arndt (1803) draws the fatherland's frontier by language; the Pan-German League and Class carry the claim into the Wilhelmine period.

national-self-determination.rationale: Arndt, Fichte and Wirth, who offers the same freedom to Poland, Hungary and Italy, hold that each people should have its own state, but the Pan-German League and Class demand expropriating and Germanising the Poles; the strands split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Arndt blames the princes' many-state polyarchy for Germany's misfortune and the National Association demands one central power and the Austrian Germans' union; a nation divided by an outside power falls under the same demand.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The Pan-German League's statutes call for preserving German ethnicity abroad and supporting it where threatened, its 1898 programme funds German schools abroad, the Frankfurt constitution puts Germans abroad under the Reich's protection, and Westarp in 1926 makes protection of German minorities in South Tyrol and Danzig a condition of joining the League of Nations.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Jahn's Volkstum, Fichte's national education and the Pan-German League's first aim all make preserving the German people's own culture and ethnicity the central task.

patriotic-education.rationale: Fichte's Addresses propose a whole-nation education to form love of the fatherland, and the Pan-German League and Army League demand schooling and training in keeping with German ethnicity and patriotism; the flag and anthem are not discussed in these texts.

sacred-nation.rationale: Fichte's Eighth Address ties the nation to the divine and to the permanence that gives individual sacrifice its meaning; Arndt's 1803 text names love of and sacrifice for the totality as the greatest idea, and the Army League cites Fichte.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Fichte argues the Germans are an original people whose language has continued without a break from the beginning, and Jahn and Arndt trace the German people to its ancient origins.

national-rebirth.rationale: Fichte's Addresses offer a wholly new national education to create a 'new self' after the nation's downfall, and Class calls for a deep renewal of a state he calls inwardly unhealthy.

culture-before-state.rationale: Fichte makes national education the means of salvation before a state is rebuilt, whereas the National Association and the Frankfurt Assembly put a central government and constitution first; the strands split.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Arndt's song and Wirth's speech describe the German land as the seat of hope, love and sympathy, and the Army League makes defending it a national duty.

conscription.rationale: The Frankfurt constitution makes military service equal for all with no substitutes, the Bochum programme calls universal compulsory service a national educational institution, Posadowsky in 1919 mourns losing it as moral education, and the Army League appeals to a 'nation in arms'.

war-builds-character.rationale: Treitschke praises the 'moral majesty' of war and the Army League seeks to keep the nation's 'manly spirit', but Herder, an early cultural nationalist, found war and conquest morally repugnant; the strands split.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Pan-German League, Class and the Society for German Colonization demand colonies, land and an aggressive foreign policy, while Wirth's democratic strand wants Germany to free other peoples rather than rule them and the National Liberal Kapp opposed colonies beyond coaling stations; the strands split.

nation-first.rationale: Class and the Army League put national power first and attack internationalism, while Wirth's Hambach speech looks to a fraternal alliance of free peoples; the strands split.

democracy-best.rationale: Wirth, the Frankfurt Basic Rights and the National Liberals' universal equal suffrage rest on popular participation, while Class calls universal equal suffrage a lie and Moeller and Jung reject party rule and formal democracy for leadership from above; the strands split.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Wirth demands rule by the will of society and the Frankfurt Assembly wrote a constitution, while Class would restrict the franchise to the propertied and educated; the strands split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Frankfurt constitution creates a hereditary Emperor and Class addresses the Kaiser, but Wirth at Hambach calls for overthrowing the kings; the strands split.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Frankfurt constitution makes the imperial dignity hereditary, while Wirth objects that peoples should not suffer 'a couple of ignorant lads' inheriting the role of king; the strands split.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Class would expel socialist deputies, officials, editors and union leaders from the Reich, while the Frankfurt Basic Rights guarantee press freedom and the right to form associations without preventive measures; the strands split.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Frankfurt constitution lets arrest, search and assembly protections be suspended in war or riot under conditions, and Class would revive Bismarck's anti-socialist law.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Frankfurt Basic Rights make all Germans equal before the law and abolish rank, while Class, the Bochum programme (Jews barred from voting and office) and Jung ('in place of equality, the inner value of the individual') reject equal standards; the strands split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Herder treats peoples as distinct cultures without ranking them, but Fichte calls the Germans the original people with the right to be called simply 'the people', and Class puts German interests first; the strands split.

religious-nation.rationale: Hasse of the Pan-German League, the Bochum programme and Jung ('Germanically Christian or not at all') tie the nation to Christianity, but the Frankfurt Basic Rights make civil rights independent of religion and Class calls religion an emanation of race; the strands split.

single-official-language.rationale: The Pan-German League's 1898 list demands banning foreign languages in clubs and meetings and Germanising schools and names, while the Frankfurt constitution guarantees equal rights for the languages of non-German peoples in church, school, administration and courts; the strands split.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Frankfurt constitution guarantees non-German peoples equal use of their languages in school, administration and courts, while the Pan-German League demanded complete Germanisation of schools and a ban on foreign languages in meetings; the strands split.

purge-loanwords.rationale: The Pan-German League's 1898 list asks to Germanise foreign words in official language, and Fichte holds that obscure foreign terms should be translated into 'right and true German'.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: List's national system argues for protective duties as the nation's industrial education, but Wirth at Hambach praises free world trade as civilisation's fruit; the strands split.

free-trade.rationale: Wirth calls free world trade the fruit of civilisation, while List argues that it benefits only nations already industrially advanced; the strands split.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Frankfurt Basic Rights call property inviolable except for the common good with compensation, while the Pan-German League and Class call for expropriating Polish landowners; the strands split.

workers-nation.rationale: The Pan-German League's president Hasse fought Social Democratic internationalism, Class wants the masses turned away from it, and the Army League attacks 'international brotherhood'; all urge working people toward the nation.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Jahn holds that the purer a people the better, Arndt hates any confluence of peoples as the road to their dissolution, and the Pan-German League urges one racial and cultural German whole.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Arndt predicts that the mixing of peoples ends in their political and moral death, and Hasse of the Pan-German League called immigration a danger to the state's German and Christian character.

notes: Strands: the Romantic strand (Fichte, Arndt, Jahn) and the 1848 liberal-democratic strand state the national question in common; the Pan-German strand of 1890-1914 shares it but adds expansion, an offensive army, Germanisation of minorities and restrictions on Jews, where the Hambach and Frankfurt texts take opposite lines; those are recorded as splits (0, low). Positions stated by the Frankfurt constitution alone (separation of powers, bicameral Reichstag, abolition of the death penalty, church-state separation, a national constituent assembly) are null because no other strand is shown to share them, and Pan-German-only positions on immigration, colonies and the economy are null for the same reason. The Nazi state and the Wilhelmine Empire's policies are not counted. Searched all themes in the Fichte, Arndt, Jahn, Frankfurt, National Association, Pan-German, Army League, Treitschke and List texts and Wertheimer's study; the main gaps are the Frankfurt Assembly's debates (Posen, Schleswig, Jewish emancipation), Treitschke's essays and Lagarde (OCR of the Fraktur was unreadable), and Max Weber's 1895 Freiburg lecture and Naumann's Mitteleuropa (no full text found). Deepen pass (2026-10-30) added the Weimar nationalist right (Moeller van den Bruck, Jung, Westarp, Posadowsky), Lagarde, the National Liberal programme, the Bochum antisemitic programme, the colonial manifesto and Kapp's reply; these turned several kept answers into stronger splits and added eight new ones. Not obtained as readable text: Siebenpfeiffer's Hambach speech, Frankfurt Assembly debates (Posen, Schleswig, Austria, emancipation), Weber 1895, Naumann's Mitteleuropa, Langbehn, the Pan-German founding appeal, the DNVP programme.
